---
title: "Probability factorization"
---

What proportion of all retained tokens are both *ne* and `obj`? If we know the proportion whose lemma is *ne* and the object proportion within those tokens, the **chain rule** reconstructs the joint probability.

We derive the two-event factorization, reverse its order, extend it to more events, and then identify where dependence remains in the conditional factors.

## The two-event chain rule

Because $\mathbb{P}(N)>0$, begin with [conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd#conditioning-as-rescaling),
which restricts the reference event and rescales its mass to one:

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O,N)}{\mathbb{P}(N)}.
$$

Multiply both sides by $\mathbb{P}(N)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(O,N)
=
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)\mathbb{P}(N).
$$

More generally, for events $B$ and $C$ with $\mathbb{P}(B)>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C\mid B).
$$

```{r}
#| label: load-factorization-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L)

is_ne <- as.logical(wh$ne_lemma)
is_object <- as.logical(wh$object)
p_ne <- mean(is_ne)
p_object_given_ne <- mean(is_object[is_ne])
p_ne_object_direct <- mean(is_ne & is_object)
p_ne_object_factored <- p_ne * p_object_given_ne

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  p_ne_object_direct,
  p_ne_object_factored
)))

c(marginal_ne = p_ne,
  conditional_object_given_ne = p_object_given_ne,
  joint_direct = p_ne_object_direct,
  joint_factored = p_ne_object_factored)
```

The count arithmetic makes the route visible:

$$
\underbrace{\frac{147}{167}}_{\text{reach }N} % dqr-allow: empirical-answer
\underbrace{\frac{112}{147}}_{\text{reach }O\text{ within }N} % dqr-allow: empirical-answer
=
\underbrace{\frac{112}{167}}_{\text{reach }N\cap O}. % dqr-allow: empirical-answer
$$
<!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

In the code, these three quantities are `p_ne`, `p_object_given_ne`, and
`p_ne_object_factored`. The cancellation is the empirical version of the
algebraic rearrangement above.

The empirical factors produce a joint probability of `r round(p_ne_object_factored, 3)`, exactly matching the directly counted intersection. This agreement is an algebraic identity, not evidence for independence.

```{r}
#| label: plot-factorization
#| fig-cap: "The marginal *ne* mass is partitioned into its observed `nsubj` and `obj` joint masses."
factor_plot <- data.frame(
  relation = c("nsubj", "obj"),
  probability = c(
    mean(is_ne & !is_object),
    mean(is_ne & is_object)
  )
)

ggplot(factor_plot, aes(relation, probability, fill = relation)) +
  geom_col(color = "white", width = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(nsubj = "grey", obj = "steelblue"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "UD relation within *ne*", y = "Joint probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Reversing the order

The same joint probability can be factored in the other order:

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
=
\mathbb{P}(O)\mathbb{P}(N\mid O).
$$

```{r}
#| label: reverse-factorization
p_object <- mean(is_object)
p_ne_given_object <- mean(is_ne[is_object])
p_reverse <- p_object * p_ne_given_object

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(p_reverse, p_ne_object_direct)))
c(forward = p_ne_object_factored, reverse = p_reverse)
```

Thus

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)\mathbb{P}(N)
=
\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)\mathbb{P}(O).
$$

We use this identity to derive [Bayes' rule](bayes-rule.qmd).

## Three-event and general chain rules

For events $B,C,D\in\mathcal F$, with the displayed conditioning events having positive probability, first write

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C)\mathbb{P}(B,C),
$$

then factor the remaining joint probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Substitution yields

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C).
$$

Repeating the same move gives the general chain rule:

$$
\mathbb{P}(E_1,\ldots,E_M)
=
\mathbb{P}(E_1)
\prod_{i=2}^{M}
\mathbb{P}(E_i\mid E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1}).
$$

The ordering is arbitrary, but every factor must condition on all preceding events in the chosen order.

To see the repeated substitution, factor the final event from the joint of the
first $M-1$ events, then factor the final event from that remaining joint, and
continue until only $\mathbb{P}(E_1)$ remains. No conditional may drop an
earlier event unless a separate conditional-independence assumption licenses
that deletion.

## Factorization and dependence

The conditional term retains any dependence between the events. Replacing
$\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ with $\mathbb{P}(O)$ requires an additional independence
assumption: conditioning on $N$ must leave the probability of $O$ unchanged.
The [independence page](independence.qmd) will show that this conditional
criterion is equivalent to a product factorization; the multiplication sign
alone supplies no such assumption.

The factorization describes the finite annotated extract. It does not show that lemma choice causes dependency relation, nor that the token rows are independent across sentences or registers.

The chain rule expands a joint probability into ordered conditional factors without assuming independence. The [next page](bayes-rule.qmd) solves the two factorizations for a reversed conditional.

## Check your understanding

1. Reconstruct $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim},O)$ from $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim})$ and $\mathbb{P}(O\mid L=\textit{kim})$.
2. Factor the same joint probability in the reverse order and verify equality in R.
3. Derive the three-event chain rule by applying the two-event rule twice.
4. Name the extra assumption needed to replace a conditional factor with its marginal counterpart.
5. A student treats the product sign in the chain rule as evidence that the
   events are independent. Which factor preserves their dependence?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim},O)=(17/167)(3/17)=3/167=0.017964$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The reverse factorization is $\mathbb{P}(O)\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim}\mid O)=(116/167)(3/116)=3/167$, equal to the same joint probability. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Applying the two-event rule twice gives $\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C,D)\mathbb{P}(C\mid D)\mathbb{P}(D)$ when the conditioning events have positive probability. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Replacing $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ with $\mathbb{P}(O)$ requires the additional assumption that $O$ and $N$ are independent. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The conditional factor $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ preserves dependence by allowing
   the object probability within $N$ to differ from the marginal object
   probability.

</details>

The two-event chain rule reconstructs a joint probability from a marginal and
a conditional. Reversing the order changes the conditional but not the joint
event, and repeated substitution yields the general rule without assuming
independence. The [next page](bayes-rule.qmd) uses the two possible orders to
reverse a conditional.
